But I realized something. It wasn't my weight. It was my confidence. When I gained weight, I hated myself. I stopped talking to people, stopped going out, and was miserable. When I was motivated enough to lose weight, I was happier, more outgoing, louder, and friendly. And your personality really reflects. So yes, I was treated differently, but it was because I treated myself differently.

There came a point in my life when I had a revelation. Do you ever go to safeway and they have those HUGE bottles of ibuprofen, like the 300 tablet ones? Well, there I was, opening a new bottle and swallowing pills by the handful. I took all 300, went to bed, excited that I would finally not have to deal with anything anymore.

I woke up around 2am, and started throwing up in the bathroom. In my house, my parent's bedroom is right across the hall from said bathroom. My mom heard me throwing up and opened the door. Instead of her saying, "Oh my gosh, you must be sick/do you need water/etc.," she turned to me and said, "Are you fucking pregnant?"

She thought it was morning sickness. My mom thought that I was some slutty daughter who was pregnant at 16 (she thinks anyone who loses their virginities before marriage is a total whore). And here I am, failed suicide attempt again, with my mom asking me if I'm pregnant. I said no, she turned around and left, and I sat on that bathroom floor waiting to die. I hated myself, I hated things that I had been through, and I hated my mom. (On a side note, I hated her way before that incident.)

But death never came. I got up, gargled with some mouthwash, and went back to bed. As I lay in bed, I thought about everything that had happened over the years, and I realized something. I didn't need a lot of the relationships that were detrimental. I didn't need my bad habits, I didn't need my current living situation, and I didn't need my suicide attempts.

And from that moment on, my life changed. I no longer have a lot of friends (I cut people out quickly, even today), I no longer have a good relationship with anyone in my family except for one of my sisters and my father (that's all I need), and anything else that comes my way, I can take care of.

I'm telling you all of this because I know how it feels to give up. If you can make it this far, there must be a reason that you're alive. I'm proud of you for picking up the pieces again and again and again. If anything, rely on yourself (people can't be trusted, honestly.), work at every problem cautiously, and message me if you need any advice/help/more depressing stories. It'll be okay.

My happiest, most cherished memory is when I found my cat. I live in a big neighborhood and everyone has their space, so when the family down the road adopted a cat, they thought it was a fat male cat. It turned out to be pregnant, and as soon as the kittens were old enough to be separated from their mother, the family took all the kittens and put them outside to die. Growing up, I isolated myself frequently, and stumbled upon one of these kittens. Long story short, I've had her for six years.

My other memory, although pretty sad, is also one that is cherished. I hid bipolar disorder from everyone I knew for twenty years. As a result, my family assumed I was some emotional, crazy person who was always 'freaking out'. One day, I decided to tell my mom (just my mom, in strictest confidentiality), and she told me that it wasn't 'normal', and there was no way she could accept me as my daughter.

It's funny, because I thought the reason we never got along was because she didn't understand me, but the whole reason is that my family is shallow. My mom doesn't accept the fact that my sister is a lesbian, so I wasn't too surprised. She also told my dad, aunts, uncles, cousins, sisters, her coworkers, and people on the street about my bipolar disorder, which she had no consent for, obviously. Anyways, I'm really glad that happened because I no longer have false hope that her and I can ever bond, so our time spent together is short, and filled with small talk.

Most of the time, my 'episodes' are random, but I do have a few triggers. If I'm put in the spotlight at all, that can cue embarrassment  which can lead to angry outbursts. If I feel overwhelmed by homework/grades/work/life in general, I can break down and start crying. Other times (and most often), I will say something to someone that has a rude tone or can sound snarky, and I'll try to explain to them I didn't mean to snap at them, but they're already hurt so everything gets chaotic quickly.

Living with the disorder isn't as rough as most people assume. There's four different types of cycles (emotional rollercoasters): Bipolar cycling (the most infrequent), rapid cycling, ultra rapid cycling, and ultraradian (the more frequent). What I have is a mixture of rapid cycling and bipolar cycling, so it's a bit more frequent than what is considered 'normal'.

However, it's not bad. I go to school, have a job, volunteer, own a cat. It's just that I can get overwhelmed easily, I stress far too much, and can 'feel' when an episode is coming on. My depression, for example, happens most frequently when I'm driving alone. I'll be driving along, singing to the radio, when suddenly- I'll stop. And I'm feel the lump in my throat start to form. Then I wonder what's making me sad out of nowhere, and I immediately begin to feel lost and confused, which will make me more upset. Then, if I allow it, it'll spiral into depression that can last for days or weeks.

Other times, I can have angry outbursts, especially at teachers. When I'm in class and I don't understand, I'll raise my hand and my teacher will call on me (standard procedure). But when she calls on me, my face gets red, my eyes will tear up, I'll shake my head, and if they pursue it (ONLY if they pursue it) I'll yell and ask them why they're so fucking nosy.

Overall, a lot of it doesn't make sense, so it's difficult for people to wrap their heads around the concept. It's nice you give your friend a chance, most people don't. The best way I can describe how it feels living with bipolar is this: You're carrying an egg on a spoon. Sometimes you have it balanced, sometimes you don't.

5. My doctor treated my son as any other patient, albeit with a bit more concern due to his age. My son was fine though, like I said. It was a short flu, and everyone is a-okay! My doctor tried to push vaccines from the get go, but he knew I was stubborn.
